stances.claim: The reader-perceived asymmetry between fast Cedric-Lee detention and slow PDAF prosecution is explained by the fundamental difference in crime structure: illegal detention (Art 167 RPC) is straightforward single-act; plunder (RA 7080) is a complicated combination or series of crimes establishing an overall scheme or conspiracy, requiring far more evidence-pinpointing per respondent.

The evidentiary truckloads on the overall scheme (NBI + COA + whistleblowers) are sufficient to prove plunder of the public treasury -- the big question is whether they pinpoint each respondent's role, particularly the three senators', which is the actual bottleneck.

Care in pinpointing whom to charge is critical because filing may result in arrest and detention, and under the Plunder Law indicted senators shall be suspended from office -- disrupting the Senate's functions, a serious institutional consequence.
Probable cause is the legal floor, but the OOO should go beyond it and make sure the evidence will convict -- a little delay can be excused provided the prosecution can eventually secure punishment.

Like the Maguindanao massacre, the pork barrel cases are a litmus test of our justice system -- the people are totally disgusted at the outrageous scam and will never forgive or forget any mishandling, cover-up, or political shenanigan; let justice be done though the heavens fall.

The implicit-reader-comparison Cedric Lee/Cornejo arrest-arraignment-fast vs Napoles-PDAF-slow -- and Panganiban's structural-not-political explanation -- the most direct address in the corpus to the reader-suspicion-of-favoritism in PDAF pace.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban addresses reader impatience over the slow PDAF prosecution against the fast Cedric Lee/Vhong Navarro detention case. The trigger: ten of the twenty Senate blue ribbon committee members have found probable cause and recommended plunder charges against Senators Jinggoy Estrada, Juan Ponce Enrile, and Bong Revilla -- and notably Estrada's half-brother Sen. JV Ejercito signed the committee report, telling Rappler 'It's the right thing to do.' To explain the pace difference, Panganiban compares the law and the evidence required. Plunder under RA 7080 is a complicated offense -- 'amasses, accumulates or acquires ill-gotten wealth [of at least P50 million] through a combination or series of overt or criminal acts' establishing an overall scheme or conspiracy, cognizable by the Sandiganbayan when committed by high-ranking officials. Illegal detention under RPC Art 167 is straightforward and uncomplicated -- 'any private individual who shall kidnap or detain another' -- committed in single acts, easy to perpetrate, investigate, and prove, cognizable by the RTC. Both are capital offenses non-bailable when evidence of guilt is strong, but plunder's structural complexity (multiple acts, multiple respondents, schemes via NGOs) means the truckloads of NBI/COA/whistleblower evidence on the overall scheme are sufficient for plunder of the treasury but the bottleneck is pinpointing each respondent's role, particularly the three senators'. He adds that care in pinpointing is critical because filing may trigger arrest and indefinite detention, and the Plunder Law's suspension-from-office consequence could disrupt Senate functioning. His prescription is the CJP-signature prudence-over-haste: while only probable cause is required to file, the OOO should go beyond and make sure evidence will convict; a little delay can be excused if it secures punishment. He invokes the Jinggoy Estrada document-furnishing petition (Morales's prompt remedy headed off SC reversal) as the model of due-process care, frames the pork cases as a litmus test like Maguindanao, and closes with the Latin maxim: Fiat justitia ruat caelum -- let justice be done though the heavens fall.
